opus-5.5.text:
I think these demonstrations are informative, but you have to read them carefully. When a model completes a task at, say, ten or a hundred times what it would cost to pay a human expert, the naive reaction is "this isn't economically relevant yet, so it doesn't matter much." I think that's mostly the wrong takeaway.

First, cost comes down really fast. Historically, once a capability exists at some price point, the cost of reaching that same level has fallen dramatically, often an order of magnitude or more per year, from algorithmic improvements, distillation, better hardware, and inference optimizations. So "possible but expensive" today is a pretty good leading indicator of "possible and cheap" a year or two out. The existence proof matters more than the price tag.

Second, it tells you something about the shape of the capability. If you can throw a lot of inference compute at a problem, with many samples, long chains of reasoning, and search, and get human-level or better performance, then the bottleneck isn't some missing ingredient. It's efficiency. That's a very different situation from "we can't do this at any price," and it's the kind of gap that tends to close.

Third, there are cases where above-human cost is already fine. If you're doing AI R&D, or something security-relevant, or anything where speed or parallelism is very valuable, paying a premium can make sense. A lab might happily spend a lot of compute to get research done faster, because the value of speeding up the frontier is enormous to them. So I wouldn't treat human cost parity as a hard threshold for when things start mattering.

That said, I want to add caveats in the other direction. Sometimes these high-cost results lean on things that don't generalize well, like best-of-N with a verifier that happens to exist for that benchmark but wouldn't exist in messy real-world tasks. In those cases, the expensive result may overstate how close we are. So I try to ask: how much of the performance comes from scaffolding and selection that relies on cheap, reliable checking, versus from the model actually being competent? And how representative is the task of the stuff we actually care about, like long-horizon, poorly specified, real research or engineering work?

So my overall interpretation is that these results are meaningful evidence that capabilities are closer than cost-adjusted metrics would suggest, which matters for timelines and for when you need safety measures in place. But you should discount somewhat for benchmark-specific tricks, and focus on what the trend in cost-for-a-given-capability looks like over time rather than any single snapshot.

r001.rationale: The response argues that above-human cost does not sharply limit usefulness or future relevance; it does not state that scaling such performance has limited scope.

r002.rationale: It says that capabilities demonstrated at high cost are likely to become cheap within a year or two as costs decline.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think these demonstrations are interesting but you have to be pretty careful about what they're actually telling you. When a lab shows a model completing some multi-hour software engineering task, or writing a research paper, or whatever, and it turns out that it cost ten times what it would have cost to pay a human to do it, I think the right reaction is not "this is useless" and it's also not "AI can do this now." It's something more like: this is evidence about where the capability frontier is, and cost is a separate axis that tends to come down fast.

So the thing I'd emphasize is that cost and capability have historically moved somewhat independently. If a model can do a task at all, even very expensively, that's a pretty strong signal that a cheaper model will be able to do it within, I don't know, a year or two. We've seen this repeatedly: the first time some capability shows up it's at the very expensive end of inference scaling, lots of samples, lots of test-time compute, maybe a bunch of scaffolding, and then eighteen months later a model that's an order of magnitude cheaper does it in one shot. So "above human cost" is a point-in-time fact that I'd expect to decay quite quickly.

That said, there are a couple of reasons to be skeptical. One is that a lot of these demonstrations involve heavy selection. You run the model a hundred times, or you let it use enormous amounts of compute, and you report the successes. If the task is one where you can verify the output cheaply, like a coding task with tests, then that's actually a fine strategy and the cost is real but the capability is real too. But if you can't verify the output, then the "success" might be partly the humans picking the good run, and that's a very different thing. So I'd ask: how much human judgment went into selecting what you're showing me?

The other thing is that the tasks are often chosen to be legible and well-specified. Real work involves a lot of context, a lot of figuring out what the task even is, and the demonstrations tend to strip that out. So I'd update more on a model doing a messy, poorly-specified task at high cost than a clean benchmark task at high cost.

But overall, if you asked me which I'd rather see as evidence about where things are going, a model doing a task at ten times human cost versus a model not being able to do the task at any cost, the first one is much scarier, or much more exciting depending on your view. The hard part is getting the capability to exist at all. Once it exists, I think the default expectation should be that it gets cheap. And that matters a lot for things like forecasting when AI can substantially automate AI research, because the relevant question there isn't really "can it do this cheaper than a human today," it's "can it do this at all, and what's the trajectory of cost."

r001.rationale: The response says above-human cost is a point-in-time fact and expects costs to fall, but does not state that high cost limits the scope for scaling the task.

r002.rationale: The response treats expensive task performance as evidence that cheaper models will soon perform it, and says the capability should become economical as costs decline.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between “the model can do this at all” and “the model can do this economically.” If you spend vastly more on a task than it would cost to hire a human, then demonstrating success doesn’t establish that you can profitably automate that work.

But it can still be evidence about capabilities. Suppose the model succeeds by trying a huge number of times. You’d want to know how you picked the successful attempt. If there’s a cheap, reliable way to check the answer, then repeated attempts might be a perfectly reasonable strategy, and the main issue is cost. If a human has to do a lot of work to identify which attempt was good, that’s a more substantial limitation.

And costs can come down, so something that’s uneconomic today could become economically relevant later. But I wouldn’t just assume that happens on a particular timeline. I’d take the demonstration as evidence that some of the capability is there, and then separately ask how much cheaper and more reliable it needs to get.

r001.rationale: It says success at a cost far above hiring a human does not establish profitable automation, limiting what the demonstration shows about economic scalability.

r002.rationale: It says a task uneconomical today could become economically relevant as costs fall, and treats the demonstration as evidence that some capability is already present.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between “Can the model do this at all?” and “Is it economically useful?” If you spend substantially more than you would pay a human, you might demonstrate the first without demonstrating the second. And even then, you want to know how much human assistance went into setting up the task, selecting attempts, and checking the result.

But I wouldn’t dismiss the demonstration. Sometimes you can get costs down a lot through improvements in the model or the way you run it. So it can be evidence that economically useful automation is getting closer, even if it isn’t there yet.

The thing I’d most want to see is the curve: how does success rate change as you spend more? If you only see one successful run with a very large budget, it’s hard to know what to infer. If you see reliable performance across a representative set of tasks, and costs are falling, that’s much stronger evidence.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes capability from economic usefulness when costs exceed human pay, but it does not state that this limits the scope for scaling.

r002.rationale: It says costs may fall with model or operational improvements and that above-cost demonstrations can be evidence that economically useful automation is getting closer.
